q: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

items.p: Every spring, volunteers at the Millbrook Nature Center count the frogs calling from the center's ponds. The counts help staff track whether the frog population is stable. This year, volunteers will also record water temperature, so that staff can study how warmer springs affect frog activity.
c: To explain what a volunteer frog count involves and why it is done
To argue that frogs are disappearing everywhere
To describe the history of the nature center
To persuade readers to visit the ponds
w: The text makes no claim about frogs everywhere.
The center's history isn't discussed.
The text informs rather than persuades.
items.e: The text describes the count, its purpose, and this year's addition.

items.q: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?
items.p: Many people think of pigeons as city birds. However, wild pigeons originally lived on rocky sea cliffs. City buildings, with their ledges and stone walls, resemble those cliffs, which may explain why pigeons thrive in cities.
c: It offers a possible reason for a pattern described earlier in the text.
It contradicts the claim made in the first sentence.
It introduces a topic unrelated to pigeons.
It gives an example of a rocky sea cliff.
w: It supports, rather than contradicts, the idea that pigeons do well in cities.
It's directly about pigeons.
It compares buildings to cliffs; it doesn't give an example of a cliff.
items.e: The third sentence explains why pigeons thrive in cities: buildings resemble their original cliff homes.

items.p: Chef Ana Lopes keeps a vegetable garden behind her restaurant. Each morning she checks what is ripe before writing the day's menu, which changes almost daily. Lopes says this habit forces her to invent new dishes and keeps her cooking from becoming routine.
c: To describe a chef's approach to planning her menu and its benefit
To argue that every restaurant should have a garden
To list the vegetables Lopes grows
To compare Lopes's restaurant with others
w: The text describes one chef; it doesn't argue for all restaurants.
No vegetables are listed.
No other restaurants are mentioned.
items.e: The text explains Lopes's garden-based menu planning and why she values it.

items.q: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
items.p: Wind turbines are usually placed on land, but some engineers now build them at sea. Winds over the ocean tend to be stronger and steadier than winds over land. As a result, offshore turbines can generate more electricity.
c: It gives a reason that supports the claim in the third sentence.
It describes a drawback of offshore turbines.
It contradicts the first sentence.
It summarizes the text as a whole.
w: Stronger winds are an advantage.
It explains the first sentence's trend rather than contradicting it.
It's a supporting reason, not a summary.
items.e: Stronger, steadier ocean winds explain why offshore turbines produce more electricity ("As a result").

items.p: Before printed maps were common, sailors in some regions memorized long chants that described coastlines, currents, and landmarks in the order they would appear. Reciting a chant during a voyage helped sailors keep track of where they were.
c: To describe how some sailors used memorized chants to navigate
To argue that chants are more accurate than maps
To explain how printed maps were invented
To describe the music sailors enjoyed
w: No comparison of accuracy is made.
The invention of maps is not explained.
The chants served navigation, not entertainment.
items.e: The text explains what the chants contained and how they helped sailors navigate.

items.q: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
items.p: The museum's new exhibit features objects from everyday life in the 1950s. Visitors can see a kitchen, a radio, and a child's bedroom furnished exactly as they would have been. Curators hope the exhibit will help younger visitors imagine their grandparents' childhoods.
c: It gives examples of what the exhibit includes.
It explains why the exhibit was created.
It criticizes the exhibit's design.
It describes the history of the museum.
w: The purpose comes in the third sentence.
No criticism is offered.
The museum's history isn't discussed.
items.e: The kitchen, radio, and bedroom are examples of the "objects from everyday life" the first sentence mentions.

items.p: Most of the moon's surface is covered in a layer of fine dust. Because the moon has almost no atmosphere, there is no wind to blow this dust away, so footprints left by astronauts decades ago are most likely still visible today.
c: To explain why footprints on the moon are likely to last a long time
To describe how astronauts trained for missions
To argue that the moon has strong winds
To compare moon dust with sand on Earth
w: Training isn't discussed.
The text says there is no wind.
Earth's sand isn't mentioned.
items.e: The text links the moon's dust and lack of wind to footprints lasting for decades.

items.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.p: Some economists predicted that a new highway would bring businesses to the small town of Lyle. When the highway opened, a few gas stations and restaurants appeared near the exit. Yet the town's main street, now bypassed by travelers, lost several shops. Overall, the town's business activity changed less than either supporters or opponents had predicted.
c: It presents a prediction, describes mixed results, and then offers an overall assessment.
It describes a problem and then proposes a solution.
It compares two towns and argues that one is better.
It presents a theory and then provides evidence that proves it.
w: No solution is proposed.
Only one town is discussed.
The results only partly matched the prediction.
items.e: The text moves from a prediction, to gains and losses, to an overall judgment.

items.q: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
items.p: Researchers once believed that the giant squid was a sluggish animal that drifted slowly in deep water. Then, in 2004, a research team photographed a giant squid attacking bait in the wild. The images showed the squid moving quickly and seizing the bait with its long tentacles.
c: It introduces evidence that challenges an earlier belief.
It restates the earlier belief in different words.
It describes the habitat where giant squid live.
It explains why the squid was thought to be sluggish.
w: It introduces new evidence rather than restating.
It's about an observation, not habitat.
It doesn't explain the old belief.
items.e: The 2004 photographs are new evidence that leads into the third sentence's challenge to the "sluggish" belief.

items.p: Grandmother kept her recipes in no book. She cooked by memory, adding a pinch of this and a handful of that, and when we asked for exact amounts she only laughed. Years later, trying to recreate her soup, I realized the recipe had lived in her hands, not in any measurement.
c: To show how the narrator came to understand the nature of the grandmother's cooking
To provide a recipe for the grandmother's soup
To criticize the grandmother for refusing to share
To describe the narrator's career as a chef
w: No recipe is given.
Her laughter is fond, not a refusal being criticized.
The narrator's career isn't mentioned.
items.e: The text builds to the narrator's realization that the recipe existed only in the grandmother's practiced hands.

items.q: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
items.p: Many coastal cities protect themselves from storms with concrete sea walls. Such walls can be effective, but they also prevent beaches from naturally replenishing their sand. Some cities are therefore experimenting with "living shorelines" of marsh grasses and oyster reefs, which absorb wave energy while preserving natural processes.
c: It identifies a drawback that motivates the alternative described next.
It argues that sea walls never work.
It describes how oyster reefs grow.
It states the text's final conclusion.
w: It grants that walls "can be effective."
Oyster reefs come later and their growth isn't described.
The text ends with the alternative, not this sentence.
items.e: The sea walls' drawback explains why cities are "therefore" trying living shorelines.

items.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.p: In the nineteenth century, many doctors dismissed the idea that washing hands could prevent disease. A few physicians who insisted on handwashing reported far fewer infections among their patients, but their findings were often ignored. Only after scientists identified germs as a cause of disease did handwashing become standard practice.
c: It describes resistance to a practice, early evidence for it, and its eventual acceptance.
It argues that doctors today still ignore handwashing.
It explains in detail how germs were discovered.
It compares two different medical treatments.
w: The text is about the past.
The discovery of germs is mentioned, not explained.
Only one practice is discussed.
items.e: The text traces a sequence: dismissal, ignored evidence, then acceptance once germs were understood.

items.q: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
items.p: Critics often praise novelist Iris Kade for her vivid settings. Yet her settings are rarely described directly. Instead, readers learn about a place through what characters notice, such as the sticky door of a café or a neighbor's radio through a wall, so that the setting emerges from the characters' attention rather than from the narrator's descriptions.
c: It introduces a qualification that the rest of the text explains.
It contradicts the critics' praise and argues that the settings are weak.
It provides an example of one of Kade's vivid descriptions.
It summarizes Kade's career.
w: It doesn't call the settings weak; it explains how they work.
The examples come in the third sentence.
Kade's career isn't discussed.
items.e: The "Yet" sentence adds a surprising qualification (settings are seldom described directly), and the next sentence explains how they come through anyway.

items.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.p: For years I measured my running by speed, logging every mile and comparing each week to the last. Then an injury forced me to walk for three months. Walking, I noticed the street I had run down a thousand times: its gardens, its cracked steps, the dog that waited at one gate. When I returned to running, I left my watch at home.
c: It describes a habit, an interruption that changed the narrator's perspective, and a resulting change in behavior.
It argues that walking is better exercise than running.
It compares two different neighborhoods.
It explains how to recover from a running injury.
w: No argument about exercise is made.
Only one street is described.
Recovery methods aren't discussed.
items.e: The text moves from an old habit, to an injury that changed what the narrator noticed, to running without a watch.

items.p: Some historians treat the diaries of nineteenth-century travelers as reliable records of the places they visited. Historian Sara Moen urges caution. Travelers, she notes, often wrote with publication in mind, exaggerating dangers to seem adventurous and borrowing descriptions from earlier books they had read.
c: To present a historian's reasons for questioning a type of historical source
To argue that travel diaries should never be studied
To describe a famous nineteenth-century journey
To explain how travel diaries were published
w: Moen urges caution, not abandonment.
No particular journey is described.
Publishing methods aren't explained.
items.e: The text gives Moen's reasons why travel diaries may be unreliable.

items.q: Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
items.p: Glass is a solid at room temperature. Nevertheless, a popular story claims that old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows downward over centuries. In fact, the uneven thickness likely came from how window glass was made at the time, and installers often placed the thicker edge at the bottom.
c: It presents a common misconception that the text then corrects.
It provides evidence for the claim in the first sentence.
It explains how glass is manufactured.
It states the text's main conclusion.
w: It describes a story that conflicts with the first sentence.
Manufacturing comes in the third sentence.
The conclusion is the correction in the third sentence.
items.e: The second sentence states the popular belief, and "In fact" introduces the correction.

items.q: Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?
items.p: When the city of Norvale planted thousands of street trees, officials emphasized the shade the trees would provide. A later study found an unexpected additional effect: blocks with more trees reported fewer complaints about noise, perhaps because leaves absorb sound or because greenery makes residents less bothered by it. The study's authors note that they cannot yet tell which explanation is correct.
c: It acknowledges a limitation in what the study shows.
It rejects both possible explanations.
It restates the officials' original goals.
It provides new evidence supporting one explanation.
w: It says they can't choose between the explanations, not that both are wrong.
The officials' goals come in the first sentence.
It offers no new evidence.
items.e: The final sentence admits that the study can't distinguish between the two explanations.

items.q: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
items.p: In the mountain village of Selva Alta, farmers once grew dozens of potato varieties. As markets began paying more for a few uniform types, many farmers switched, and the older varieties nearly vanished. Recently, a farmers' cooperative has begun selling the rare varieties to restaurants, which value their unusual colors and flavors, giving farmers a reason to plant them again.
c: It describes a decline in crop diversity, its cause, and a development that may reverse it.
It argues that restaurants should buy only rare potatoes.
It compares potato farming in two different villages.
It explains how potatoes were first domesticated.
w: No argument is made about what restaurants should do.
Only one village is discussed.
Domestication isn't mentioned.
items.e: The text traces a loss of varieties, its market-driven cause, and a new market that may bring them back.
